title: The sentence bracket and field positions
topic_en: The sentence bracket and field positions
schema: english-prompt -> learner types German -> Reveal/Hide answer shows reference + speaker

exercises.english: Tomorrow morning the train leaves at six.
exercises.german: Morgen früh fährt der Zug um sechs ab.
exercises.why: A fronted time expression takes position I, so the finite verb fährt follows in position II and the subject comes last; the separable prefix ab stays at the very end in position III.

exercises.english: At nine o'clock the museum opens.
exercises.german: Um neun Uhr öffnet das Museum.
exercises.why: The fronted time phrase occupies position I and the conjugated verb öffnet is promoted to position II, with das Museum as the subject behind it.

exercises.english: Yesterday I read all day long.
exercises.german: Gestern habe ich den ganzen Tag gelesen.
exercises.why: Fronting Gestern forces Perfekt order: position I = Gestern, position II = habe, position III = gelesen, and the subject ich plus the time span follow.

exercises.english: The guests only arrived after dinner.
exercises.german: Erst nach dem Essen kamen die Gäste.
exercises.why: The focus particle erst belongs in position I together with nach dem Essen, and the verb kamen then takes position II before the subject die Gäste.

exercises.english: Only two colleagues understood the lecture.
exercises.german: Nur zwei Kollegen haben den Vortrag verstanden.
exercises.why: Nur is fronted with its quantified phrase, so the finite Perfekt auxiliary haben stands in position II and verstanden closes the verb bracket in position III.

exercises.english: I would love to come along.
exercises.german: Sehr gern komme ich mit.
exercises.why: With modal verbs the modal in position II carries the tense, so the whole verb bracket is komme ich and the separable prefix mit comes last in position III.

exercises.english: In good weather we are having a picnic.
exercises.german: Bei gutem Wetter machen wir ein Picknick.
exercises.why: The fronted prepositional phrase in position I leaves position II for machen, and the subject wir plus accusative object follow in that order.

exercises.english: In summer we go to the Baltic Sea.
exercises.german: Im Sommer fahren wir an die Ostsee.
exercises.why: Im Sommer is fronted, so fahren moves to position II and wir is pushed behind it; the directional complement stays at the end of the sentence.

exercises.english: The day after tomorrow we have to pay the bill.
exercises.german: Übermorgen müssen wir die Rechnung zahlen.
exercises.why: With a modal in position II the modal müssen counts as the finite verb, so the subject wir lands in position III and the infinitive zahlen ends the bracket.

exercises.english: I live in a shared flat with my sister.
exercises.german: Mit meiner Schwester wohne ich in einer WG.
exercises.why: The accompanying person is fronted, which pushes wohne into position II and leaves ich as the subject in the field behind it.

exercises.english: He has been learning Japanese for two years.
exercises.german: Seit zwei Jahren lernt er Japanisch.
exercises.why: A fronted duration phrase in position I allows present tense lernt in position II instead of a Perfekt, with er following directly.

exercises.english: This week I simply have no time.
exercises.german: Diese Woche habe ich überhaupt keine Zeit.
exercises.why: Diese Woche in position I pushes the Perfekt auxiliary habe to position II, and the negation überhaupt keine Zeit follows the subject.

exercises.english: In the end he did win after all.
exercises.german: Am Ende hat er doch noch gewonnen.
exercises.why: A fronted time phrase plus Perfekt gives Am Ende in position I, hat in position II, and gewonnen seals position III before the subject er.

exercises.english: Without an ID card you cannot get in here.
exercises.german: Ohne Ausweis kommt man hier nicht hinein.
exercises.why: The preposition ohne with its nominal complement is fronted; kommt is then the finite verb in position II and the impersonal man follows it.

exercises.english: In two years I want to work in Zürich.
exercises.german: In zwei Jahren will ich in Zürich arbeiten.
exercises.why: Modal will takes position II because the fronted time phrase fills position I, so the infinitive arbeiten goes to the end of the sentence.

exercises.english: I would gladly drink a coffee.
exercises.german: Trinken würde ich gern einen Kaffee.
exercises.why: The infinitive itself is fronted; under the special inversion the finite verb würde then moves up to position I and the subject ich follows in position II.

exercises.english: Do I really have to read the whole report?
exercises.german: Muss ich wirklich den ganzen Bericht lesen?
exercises.why: In a yes-no question the finite verb is the very first element even without any fronting, and the subject ich comes right after it in position II.

exercises.english: Careful, the floor is slippery!
exercises.german: Vorsicht, der Boden ist glatt!
exercises.why: An imperative with a fronted warning word is read as two sentences, so the verb ist begins the second clause and the subject der Boden comes after it.

exercises.english: What you find in it is for you alone to decide.
exercises.german: Was du darin findest, entscheidest nur du.
exercises.why: A fronted subordinate clause pushes the main-clause verb to position I, so entscheidest steht before the subject du, which now ends the sentence.

exercises.english: I do not know whether he is coming.
exercises.german: Dass er kommt, weiß ich nicht.
exercises.why: Fronting the dass-clause puts the verb of the main clause in position I: weiß in I, ich in II, and the negation nicht follows the subject.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: The train arrives at two p.m.
exercises.german: Der Zug kommt um vierzehn Uhr an.
exercises.why: The separable prefix an cannot stand in the middle of the verb bracket, so it detaches and occupies the final slot in position III.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Please call me back tomorrow!
exercises.german: Ruft mich bitte morgen wieder an!
exercises.why: In the imperative the pronoun object sits in position III and the particle an has to jump over it to the end of the sentence.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Have you already paid the bill?
exercises.german: Hast du die Rechnung schon bezahlt?
exercises.why: A Perfekt question puts the auxiliary hast in I and du in II; the whole participle phrase die Rechnung schon bezahlt forms the verb bracket ending in III.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: We are meeting at eight at the main station.
exercises.german: Wir treffen uns um acht am Hauptbahnhof.
exercises.why: The reflexive pronoun uns occupies position III directly after treffen, while the time and place complements are free to follow in the Nachfeld.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: The club has cancelled the game.
exercises.german: Der Verein hat das Spiel abgesagt.
exercises.why: In the Perfekt the conjugated part hat takes position II and the participle abgesagt must be pulled to the end, separating ab and gesagt.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Why do you always call me at night?
exercises.german: Warum rufst du mich nachts immer an?
exercises.why: The prefix an is stressed in meaning and therefore detaches; with two objects in position III, mich and nachts immer, the particle an comes last.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: I get up at six every morning.
exercises.german: Ich stehe jeden Morgen um sechs auf.
exercises.why: The non-finite position III cannot be filled by the separable prefix, so auf ends the sentence even though temporal phrases could stand earlier.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: She has already handed in her notice.
exercises.german: Sie hat ihre Stelle schon gekündigt.
exercises.why: Perfekt of a separable verb: hat in position II, the object ihre Stelle and the temporal schon in position III, and the participle gekündigt closes the sentence.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: He picked up the parcel at the post office.
exercises.german: Er hat das Paket bei der Post abgeholt.
exercises.why: The Perfekt auxiliary hat sits in position II, das Paket and bei der Post fill the middle field, and the participle abgeholt closes the bracket.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: He will pick you up at twelve.
exercises.german: Er holt dich um zwölf ab.
exercises.why: Future meaning is expressed by present tense holt in position II, and the separable prefix ab detaches to the very end despite the time expression.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Does the film start at half past eight?
exercises.german: Fängt der Film um halb neun an?
exercises.why: In the yes-no question an sits at the far end of the bracket, not directly after the conjugated verb, which is the classic test of position III.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: We signed the contract last week.
exercises.german: Wir haben den Vertrag letzte Woche unterschrieben.
exercises.why: The separable prefix of the participle underschrieben is torn off and forms the final element, while den Vertrag occupies position III with the temporal phrase.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Will you give me the documents tonight?
exercises.german: Gibst du mir die Unterlagen heute Abend?
exercises.why: Both pronouns and the accusative object fill the bracket positions after the imperative, and the time expression is pushed to the Nachfeld.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: How long does the meeting last?
exercises.german: Wie lange hat die Besprechung gedauert?
exercises.why: The fronted question phrase is position I, the Perfekt auxiliary hat takes position II, and the participle gedauert closes the bracket in position III.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: The children played in the garden all afternoon.
exercises.german: Die Kinder haben den ganzen Nachmittag im Garten gespielt.
exercises.why: The object and the adverbial both sit in the bracketed middle field, and the participle gespielt must be the last element of the sentence.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: On Monday I am starting the new job.
exercises.german: Am Montag fange ich die neue Stelle an.
exercises.why: The fronted day makes the present tense fange mean a future start, and the separable prefix an again occupies position III at the end.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Please sit down for a moment!
exercises.german: Setz dich bitte kurz hin!
exercises.why: The pronoun sich stands in position III and the separable prefix hin has to cross it, so the accusative-adverbial bitte kurz cannot follow the verb directly.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Can you reach me after work?
exercises.german: Kannst du mich nach der Arbeit erreichen?
exercises.why: A modal in position II leaves the infinitive erreichen at the end, which is position III; with a modal the prefix is no longer separable.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Are you taking the train or the bike?
exercises.german: Nimmst du den Zug oder das Fahrrad?
exercises.why: The two coordinated objects fill the positions after the verb, and there is no non-finite element, so position III ends with the last alternative.

exercises.skill: Position III: separable verbs and Perfekt
exercises.english: Have you talked to her yet?
exercises.german: Hast du mit ihr schon gesprochen?
exercises.why: The prepositional object mit ihr and the short temporal schon share the middle field, and the participle gesprochen anchors the end of the verb bracket.

exercises.english: In my opinion I should apologise after all.
exercises.german: Meines Erachtens sollte ich mich doch entschuldigen.
exercises.why: The stance phrase meines Erachtens occupies position I, so the modal sollte goes to position II and the reflexive sich plus the infinitive entschuldigen fill the bracket.

exercises.english: I spoke with my boss yesterday.
exercises.german: Ich habe gestern mit meiner Chefin gesprochen.
exercises.why: The Nachfeld is the optional slot after the verb bracket: gesprochen ends the sentence and the prepositional object mit meiner Chefin is the free element behind it.

exercises.english: We have to pay the bill before the end of the month.
exercises.german: Wir müssen die Rechnung vor dem Monatsende bezahlen.
exercises.why: Moving vor dem Monatsende behind the closing infinitive shows the Nachfeld at work: it belongs outside the bracket and carries the deadline.

exercises.english: The new colleague is joining us next month.
exercises.german: Der neue Kollege kommt im nächsten Monat zu uns.
exercises.why: The directional complement zu uns is the focus and therefore placed in the Nachfeld after the temporal phrase, which is also permitted but less marked.

exercises.english: You should talk to the doctor about it.
exercises.german: Du solltest mit dem Arzt darüber sprechen.
exercises.why: The prepositional object mit dem Arzt follows the modal in the bracket, while the pronoun complement darüber is a typical Nachfeld element after the infinitive.

exercises.english: He got the message last night.
exercises.german: Er hat die Nachricht gestern am Abend bekommen.
exercises.why: Placing the time expression gestern am Abend behind bekommen is possible because that is exactly the function of the Nachfeld: extending and commenting on what is already said.

exercises.english: We are meeting behind the station.
exercises.german: Wir treffen uns hinter dem Bahnhof.
exercises.why: The place complement can be moved in front of the verb, but only in the Nachfeld does it follow the whole bracket and thus close the sentence.

exercises.english: I waited for him for a long time.
exercises.german: Ich habe lange auf ihn gewartet.
exercises.why: Both den ganzen Tag and auf ihn sit inside the bracket; the Nachfeld after gewartet stays free for any further comment, which is what makes its position so flexible.

exercises.english: Have you already read the report completely?
exercises.german: Haben Sie den Bericht schon vollständig gelesen?
exercises.why: The formal pronoun Sie in position II pushes den Bericht into position III, whereas schon and vollständig are manner and temporal elements that could also go to the Nachfeld.

exercises.english: My parents are coming to visit on Sunday.
exercises.german: Meine Eltern kommen am Sonntag zu Besuch.
exercises.why: The Nachfeld noun phrase zu Besuch is the semantically decisive part of the sentence and is placed after the closing element to end the statement.

exercises.english: The lecture starts in five minutes.
exercises.german: Die Vorlesung fängt in fünf Minuten an.
exercises.why: The temporal phrase could occupy position I, but after the verb it belongs to the Nachfeld, and the separable prefix an closes the sentence.

exercises.english: We rented a small flat in the summer.
exercises.german: Wir haben im Sommer eine kleine Wohnung gemietet.
exercises.why: Placing eine kleine Wohnung at the end of the middle field puts focus on the object, which is an alternative to moving it into the Nachfeld after gemietet.

exercises.english: He was very pleased about the news.
exercises.german: Er hat sich über die Nachricht sehr gefreut.
exercises.why: The degree adverb sehr could close the sentence in the Nachfeld; here it stands inside the bracket and the position III is filled by the participle.

exercises.english: On Friday my brother is going to Leipzig.
exercises.german: Am Freitag fährt mein Bruder nach Leipzig.
exercises.why: The destination nach Leipzig closes the sentence as a Nachfeld element, which is the normal place for a directional complement with a motion verb.

exercises.english: The children played in the garden all day.
exercises.german: Die Kinder haben den ganzen Tag im Garten gespielt.
exercises.why: A long adverbial such as den ganzen Tag pushes the other field element into the Nachfeld; here im Garten keeps the balanced bracket and gespielt ends the sentence.

exercises.english: We will cover the topic next semester.
exercises.german: Wir werden das Thema im nächsten Semester behandeln.
exercises.why: The subject of the modal clause stays behind the modal, and the temporal complement can be extended into the Nachfeld after the infinitive behandeln.

exercises.english: This motion still has to be discussed in the committee.
exercises.german: Über diesen Antrag muss noch im Ausschuss gesprochen werden.
exercises.why: In the passive the participle gesprochen werden always ends the sentence, and the prepositional phrase im Ausschuss is what the Nachfeld can carry before it.

exercises.english: Have you already packed the toothbrush in the suitcase?
exercises.german: Hast du die Zahnbürste schon in den Koffer gepackt?
exercises.why: The Nachfeld is free for the prepositional object in den Koffer, but placing it there before the participle is equally correct because position III is closed by gepackt.

exercises.english: Luckily nothing happened to anyone.
exercises.german: Zum Glück ist niemandem etwas passiert.
exercises.why: Zum Glück is a comment that can sit in the middle field like an extended attribute; between subject and predicate it makes the statement sound reflective.

exercises.english: He was still standing at the station shortly before midnight.
exercises.german: Er stand tatsächlich kurz vor Mitternacht noch am Bahnhof.
exercises.why: The two long temporal phrases almost fill the middle field, so the place complement am Bahnhof is naturally pushed to the end, where the Nachfeld also allows it.

exercises.english: She has been working at a Berlin clinic since last year.
exercises.german: Seit letztem Jahr arbeitet sie in einer Berliner Klinik.
exercises.why: The duration in position I allows present tense, and the place complement in einer Berliner Klinik closes the middle field after the subject.

exercises.english: In my opinion he has the advantage.
exercises.german: Der Meinung nach ist er im Vorteil.
exercises.why: A stance phrase behaves like a fronted adverbial, so the finite verb ist moves to position II and the subject er follows it.

exercises.english: In my view we have to postpone the project.
exercises.german: Meines Erachtens müssen wir das Projekt verschieben.
exercises.why: The genitive phrase meines Erachtens fills position I and the modal müssen is promoted to position II, with wir as the subject of the following field.

exercises.english: In my view the task is too difficult.
exercises.german: Meiner Ansicht nach ist die Aufgabe zu schwer.
exercises.why: Unlike a subordinate clause, the phrase meiner Ansicht nach stays in the main clause and triggers inversion: ist in II, die Aufgabe in III.

exercises.english: In my opinion the railway should run more often.
exercises.german: Meiner Meinung nach sollte die Bahn häufiger fahren.
exercises.why: A stance phrase in position I places the modal sollte second and leaves the infinitive fahren, together with the comparative, in the closing positions.

exercises.english: I have a feeling he will be late.
exercises.german: Meinem Gefühl nach kommt er zu spät.
exercises.why: The dative stance phrase meinem Gefühl nach is field I; the verb kommt follows in II and the subject er is inserted after it.

exercises.english: I am convinced that we lack the time.
exercises.german: Meiner Überzeugung nach fehlt uns die Zeit.
exercises.why: Here the fronted stance phrase explains why the following clause sounds subjective: fehlt occupies position II and the subject comes after the verb, not before it.

exercises.english: In my opinion the company has too few trains.
exercises.german: Der Meinung nach hat der Betrieb zu wenige Züge.
exercises.why: The negated quantifier zu wenige is part of the middle field, while position I is taken by the stance phrase and position II by hat.

exercises.english: In my opinion one should rewrite the rule.
exercises.german: Meines Erachtens hat man die Regel neu schreiben.
exercises.why: With the Perfekt of a modal verb the modal-like auxiliary hat takes position II, the impersonal man follows, and the participle schreiben seals position III.

exercises.english: In my view the sender was a bot.
exercises.german: Meiner Ansicht nach war der Absender ein Bot.
exercises.why: Position I is the stance phrase, position II the copula war, and the two nominal components follow as subject and predicative complement.

exercises.english: In my view one should have acted earlier.
exercises.german: Meiner Ansicht nach hätte man früher eingreifen müssen.
exercises.why: The Konjunktiv II auxiliary hätte goes to position II, the modal infinitive must form the end of the bracket, and the participle eingreifen sits just before it.

exercises.english: In my opinion the order arrives too late.
exercises.german: Der Meinung nach kommt die Bestellung zu spät.
exercises.why: A stance phrase in first position never blocks inversion: kommt is the finite verb in II, the subject die Bestellung follows and zu spät closes the sentence.

exercises.english: I have a feeling you spelled the name wrong.
exercises.german: Meinem Gefühl nach hast du den Namen falsch geschrieben.
exercises.why: The dative phrase occupies field I, so the Perfekt auxiliary hast appears in II and the participle geschrieben ends the bracket in III.

exercises.english: I am convinced the invoice is not correct.
exercises.german: Meiner Überzeugung nach stimmt die Rechnung nicht.
exercises.why: Again the stance phrase signals that what follows is an opinion, and it still obeys the bracket rule with stimmt in II and the negation in III.

exercises.english: In my opinion that is not a good solution.
exercises.german: Meiner Meinung nach ist das keine gute Lösung.
exercises.why: After the fronted phrase the copula ist is the finite verb, das becomes the subject, and keine gute Lösung completes the sentence.

exercises.english: In my view the preliminary phase took too long.
exercises.german: Meines Erachtens hat der Vorlauf zu lange gedauert.
exercises.why: The stance phrase pushes the Perfekt auxiliary hat to position II, and the separable prefix of the participle returns to the end of the bracket as gedauert.

exercises.english: In my view the appointment could be postponed.
exercises.german: Meiner Ansicht nach könnte man den Termin verschieben.
exercises.why: The Konjunktiv II modal könnte in position II marks the hypothetical, and the object den Termin plus the separable verb verschieben fill the rest of the bracket.

exercises.english: In my opinion we have to change the law.
exercises.german: Der Meinung nach müssen wir das Gesetz ändern.
exercises.why: A stance phrase does not create a subordinate clause, so müssen takes position II directly and the infinitive ändern goes to the end.

exercises.english: According to the rumour the company is selling its site.
exercises.german: Dem Gerücht nach verkauft die Firma ihren Standort.
exercises.why: The dative source phrase dem Gerücht nach is a free position I element, and verkauft as the finite verb is then followed by the subject die Firma.

exercises.english: In my opinion the preliminary meeting was a waste of time.
exercises.german: Meiner Meinung nach war die Vorbereitung eine Zeitverschwendung.
exercises.why: Here the stance phrase in field I makes the copula war the second position, and the two nominative-style components follow in subject-predicate order.

exercises.english: The more one practises, the more confident one becomes.
exercises.german: Je mehr man übt, desto sicherer wird man.
exercises.why: The je-clause keeps normal order, but the second half is a main clause and therefore needs inversion: wird in II and man in III.

exercises.english: The later you start, the more stress you get.
exercises.german: Je später man anfängt, desto mehr Stress bekommt man.
exercises.why: The comparison must start with je; after the comma the second half inverts to bekommt man, and the two halves may not be swapped.

exercises.english: The longer you wait, the more expensive the ticket becomes.
exercises.german: Je länger man wartet, desto teurer wird das Ticket.
exercises.why: The comparative destination desto teurer introduces an ordinary main clause, so wird takes position II and das Ticket follows it.

exercises.english: The faster we drive, the earlier we arrive.
exercises.german: Je schneller wir fahren, desto früher kommen wir an.
exercises.why: The subject wir is repeated in both halves, and only the second half needs the inverted verb pair kommen wir, with an detaching to the end.

exercises.english: The less you plan, the more problems there are.
exercises.german: Je weniger man plant, desto mehr Probleme entstehen.
exercises.why: The result clause entstehen follows the comparative normally; the point of the item is that no subject-verb inversion like Probleme entstehen is possible in German.

exercises.english: The more precisely you calculate, the smaller the difference becomes.
exercises.german: Je genauer man rechnet, desto kleiner wird die Differenz.
exercises.why: The second half must be a main clause with the verb in position II, so wird comes directly after desto kleiner and not after die Differenz.

exercises.english: The more often you repeat the words, the better they stick.
exercises.german: Je öfter man die Wörter wiederholt, desto besser bleiben sie hängen.
exercises.why: The second clause inverts to bleiben sie, and the separable verb hängen detaches to the very end as position III.

exercises.english: The better you prepare, the more calmly the talk goes.
exercises.german: Je besser man sich vorbereitet, desto ruhiger läuft der Vortrag.
exercises.why: The first half contains the reflexive pronoun in the middle field, the second half inverts the verb läuft in front of its subject der Vortrag.

exercises.english: The more details you give, the clearer the matter becomes.
exercises.german: Je mehr Details man nennt, desto klarer wird die Sache.
exercises.why: The genitive detail in the first half stays in its position, whereas the result clause uses wird in position II followed by its subject.

exercises.english: The more expensive the flat is, the harder financing becomes.
exercises.german: Je teurer die Wohnung ist, desto schwerer wird die Finanzierung.
exercises.why: Both halves are main clauses, so the second one inverts to wird die Finanzierung; the comparative word order je then desto is obligatory.

exercises.english: The more precisely you plan, the better it goes.
exercises.german: Je genauer man plant, umso besser klappt es.
exercises.why: With umso the second half still needs inversion, so klappt comes before the impersonal es instead of after it.

exercises.english: The harder you train, the greater your endurance.
exercises.german: Je härter man trainiert, desto größer wird die Ausdauer.
exercises.why: The inversion in the second half is what makes it a main clause, and the subject die Ausdauer must stand behind the verb wird.

exercises.english: The longer delivery takes, the more dissatisfied the customers are.
exercises.german: Je länger die Lieferung dauert, desto unzufriedener sind die Kunden.
exercises.why: The result clause inverts to sind die Kunden, and the comparative unzufriedener comes before the verb because it is part of the predicative position.

exercises.english: The sooner you set off, the sooner you arrive.
exercises.german: Je eher du losgehst, desto eher kommst du an.
exercises.why: The second clause is again a main clause, so kommst du is inverted and the separable prefix an closes the sentence in position III.

exercises.english: The more we try, the better the result becomes.
exercises.german: Je mehr wir uns bemühen, desto besser wird das Ergebnis.
exercises.why: The reflexive sich in the first half must not be confused with the subject order in the second, where wird precedes das Ergebnis.

exercises.english: The more you study, the less you forget.
exercises.german: Je mehr man lernt, desto weniger vergisst man.
exercises.why: The result clause inverts to vergisst man, and the negating prefix ver- plus the participle vergisst stay together at the end of the bracket.

exercises.english: The higher the price, the greater the benefit.
exercises.german: Je höher der Preis ist, desto größer ist der Nutzen.
exercises.why: The second half is a full main clause, so ist occupies position II and the subject der Nutzen must follow it, never stand in front of it.

exercises.english: The later summer gets, the earlier the sun sets.
exercises.german: Je später der Sommer wird, desto früher geht die Sonne unter.
exercises.why: The inversion pattern geht die Sonne in the second half shows that this is a main clause, and the separable prefix unter detaches to position III.

exercises.english: The more rehearsals we do, the more confident the performance.
exercises.german: Je mehr Proben wir machen, desto sicherer wird die Aufführung.
exercises.why: The second half could be completed by a verb, and once wird is inserted the subject die Aufführung has to follow it, never precede it.

exercises.english: The more carefully you work, the fewer mistakes you make.
exercises.german: Je sorgfältiger man arbeitet, desto weniger Fehler entstehen.
exercises.why: German never allows Fehler entstehen in the second half; the inversion entstehen Fehler with fewer as the subject is what the item tests.
